news.content_original: Abstract In November 2025, Ethiopia reported its first outbreak of Marburg virus disease, with a case fatality rate of 64%. Here we report the analysis of seven near-complete Marburg virus genomes from seven early cases. The outbreak lineage belonged to the MARV.A.1 clade, which is closely related to genomes from historical human cases and bats. A high nucleotide identity across the seven genomes suggests human-to-human transmission after a zoonotic spillover event. These findings highlight the importance of genomic surveillance for outbreak detection, response and preparedness. Similar content being viewed by others Main Marburg virus disease (MVD) is a severe and highly lethal zoonotic infection with case fatality rates ranging from 23% to 90%1,2. It is caused by the orthomarburg viruses (Orthomarburgvirus marburgense), Marburg virus (MARV) and Ravn virus (RAVV), which belong to the Filoviridae family and are closely related to ebolaviruses, which share similar clinical features and transmission routes. Human infection typically follows zoonotic exposure in caves or mines that are inhabited by the fruit bat Rousettus aegyptiacus, with subsequent spread through direct contact with contaminated bodily fluids. The MARV genome is a single-stranded negative-sense RNA of approximately 19 kb encoding seven proteins, including nucleoprotein (NP), viral protein (VP)35, VP40, VP30, VP24, glycoprotein (GP) and the large polymerase protein (L). Since 2008, MARV has caused most documented MVD outbreaks globally and has been detected in all countries where MVD occurs, whereas RAVV has only been reported in Uganda, Kenya and the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC)1. As of March 2025, 608 confirmed cases and 453 deaths have been recorded across 19 outbreaks, predominantly in Africa3. The largest outbreak occurred in Angola in 2004–2005, resulting in 227 deaths among 252 cases. Uganda has experienced multiple outbreaks, often linked to miners exposed to bat colonies, while Kenya and the DRC reported outbreaks in the 1980s and early 2000s. More recent outbreaks in Guinea (2021), Ghana (2022), Equatorial Guinea (2023), Tanzania (2023 and 2025) and Rwanda (2024) highlight MARV’s expanding geographic footprint across East and West Africa2,3. Genomic analyses consistently show limited within-outbreak diversity, with most outbreaks arising from single zoonotic spillover events followed by human-to-human transmission1,2. Recent outbreaks in Rwanda and Tanzania involved lineages closely related to Ugandan bat-derived clades, suggesting long-term viral persistence in bat reservoirs with periodic spillover4,5. The first recorded MARV outbreak in Ethiopia was detected on 14 November 2025 following a cluster of haemorrhagic fever cases in Jinka, Ari Zone, South Ethiopia Regional State (the town, administrative zone and region, respectively)6 (Fig. 1a). Within 48 h, MVD was confirmed in suspected cases by reverse transcription PCR (RT–PCR) at the Ethiopian Public Health Institute (EPHI), with subsequent rapid implementation of a comprehensive emergency response by the government, which included contact tracing, isolation, expanded diagnostic capacity, community engagement and the deployment of antiviral drugs and vaccines. By the end of the outbreak in December 2025, 4,006 individuals were investigated, and 155 suspected cases were identified. Overall, 14 were confirmed, 9 of whom had died (case fatality rate: 64%). Three confirmed cases originating from Jinka were later detected in Hawassa, Dasenech and Malle, all with documented epidemiological links to the initial cluster. Most patients were young male adults (8 out 14 male) (Extended Data Table 1). Genomic characterization was undertaken to investigate viral evolution and transmission dynamics. Out of 14 RT–PCR-confirmed specimens, 7 samples had sufficient material and underwent whole-genome sequencing. Seven near-complete genomes were generated with ≥30× coverage that enabled confident consensus calling for >90% of the genome, applying a majority consensus rule to a minimum of ten unique reads (Extended Data Table 2). The GC content ranged from 40.2% to 41.0%. To contextualize the Ethiopian outbreak, the seven genomes were analysed along with all publicly available complete orthomarburgvirus sequences from GenBank (n = 103). Maximum-likelihood phylogenetic analysis placed all Ethiopian sequences within a single monophyletic lineage nested in the MARV.A.1 clade (Fig. 1b). To investigate the temporal origins of the 2025 Ethiopian outbreak lineage, we performed a global molecular clock analysis using the Bayesian Evolutionary Analysis Sampling Trees (BEAST). Bayesian phylogenetic analyses converged successfully, with all estimated parameters achieving effective sample size (ESS) values above the recommended threshold of 200 (Supplementary Table 1), indicating that the Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) adequately sampled the parameter space. The global MARV phylogeny exhibited a detectable temporal signal (R2 = 0.56, 1.75 × 10−4 substitutions per site per year, P < 0.001) (Extended Data Fig. 1). The Ethiopian lineage was most closely related to the human MARV isolate JN408064 (‘Leiden’ strain), isolated from a Dutch patient infected in 2008 after visiting Python Cave in Uganda7 (Fig. 1c). The estimated time to the most recent common ancestor (tMRCA) of the Ethiopian lineage and JN408064 was approximately September 1994 (95% highest posterior density (HPD) January 1993–April 1996). The lineage also clustered near the MARV sequences from the DRC (1999) and Uganda (2012)8,9. The tMRCA of the Ethiopian lineage and its closest bat-derived isolates (JX458853 and JX458858) was approximately September 1990 (95% HPD April 1987–February 1994). These bat isolates were sampled in 2008–2009 from Python Cave8. The JN408064 strain itself is closely related to the EF446132 strain responsible for the initial Marburg outbreak (1967), which also originated in Uganda10. Overall, the Ethiopian lineage exhibited extremely limited diversity, with 0–6 single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) between genomes (Extended Data Table 3). A total of 148 lineage-defining substitutions were identified, including 110 within coding DNA sequence (CDS) regions (28 non-synonymous and 82 synonymous) and 38 in intergenic regions (Fig. 2, Extended Data Table 4 and Supplementary Table 2). Most genes exhibited low non-synonymous to synonymous substitution rate ratios (dN/dS, ω) across the viral genome (Extended Data Table 5). The GP gene was the major hotspot of divergence, containing 13 fixed non-synonymous substitutions. These included Q205K in the receptor-binding domain and 11 substitutions in or near the mucin-like domain (K222N, D250N, A284T, S291P, P295L, N310D, G317D, H336R, T343I, K465E and S485P). The N501H substitution was identified in the membrane fusion region. VP35 contained a single non-synonymous substitution (S193A). The L gene contained nine substitutions (A115V, I359V, I1643T, Q1787R, P1796S, D1806N, R2091K, K2156Q and V2278A), representing the second-highest level of non-synonymous substitutions. NP and VP genes showed minimal diversity, reflecting strong functional constraint. Global MARV genomes exhibit similar patterns with low diversity in NP and VP regions and higher diversity in GP and L genes (Extended Data Fig. 2). Epidemiological investigations support that the Ethiopian outbreak originated from a single zoonotic spillover event. The earliest cases most likely contracted the infection from an index patient, who probably died from viral haemorrhagic fever in October 2025. Retrospective outbreak investigations, including the sampling of bats and fruit bats in surrounding areas, suggested that the index case had prior exposure to these animals. Between 12 and 24 November, MARV spread among close contacts of the early cases. The findings reported here represent only a fraction of the likely transmission chain, as several suspected MVD cases died before PCR confirmation, and only seven complete genomes were recovered. Indeed, this limited genomic dataset restricts our ability to robustly determine whether the genomic transmission patterns fully support the observed epidemiological links. The Ethiopian lineage’s high conservation mirrors patterns observed in recent Rwanda and Tanzania outbreaks4,5. By contrast, the 1998–2000 DRC outbreak involved multiple independent spillovers and distinct co-circulating clades11. The close relationship between the Ethiopian genomes and historical MARV.A.1 sequences suggests long-term persistence of this clade in East and Central Africa, probably maintained in bat reservoirs with occasional spillover2,8. Given the capacity of Rousettus aegyptiacus for long-distance migration, these bats may facilitate the spread of MARV across regions, including the potential establishment of endemicity in southwestern Ethiopia. The estimated ~30-year divergence of the Ethiopian lineage from its closest relatives suggests either recent introduction from neighbouring countries or cryptic circulation within Ethiopian bat populations over decades. Distinguishing between these scenarios requires expanded longitudinal surveillance. Filovirus persistence in survivors is a recognized concern, and its RNA has been detected in immune-privileged sites, including the testes12,13. MARV persistence has been reported in a Kenyan survivor 2 months post-recovery13. Although sexual transmission has not been confirmed, persistence may contribute to sporadic re-emergence. Nonetheless, most MARV outbreaks arise from new zoonotic spillovers associated with human–animal interface activities1,2. The Ethiopian outbreak exhibited only 28 non-synonymous SNPs, reflecting a highly conserved genome. All genomes showed a dN/dS < 1, consistent with strong functional constraint14. Although purifying selection is more readily detectable in ebolaviruses owing to deeper sampling and longer transmission chains, MARV’s limited diversity and sparse genomic data reduce power to observe similar patterns15. The slower evolutionary rate observed in the Ethiopian outbreak suggests that these isolates may represent stable targets for therapeutics and vaccines. Indeed, these genomic insights informed the implementation of investigational interventions, including remdesivir and Sabin’s cAd3-MARV vaccine, which was administered to patients and healthcare professionals as both therapeutic and prophylactic treatments during the outbreak period. Genomic characterization of MARV in Ethiopia reveals a lineage closely related to East African clades and probably originating from a single zoonotic spillover event. Genomic epidemiology provided actionable insights into evolutionary stability, potential sources of infection and intervention strategies. However, the findings should be interpreted with caution. The broad and partially overlapping HPD intervals observed throughout the time-scaled phylogenetic analysis might reflect several inherent limitations. These include the small sample size, short outbreak duration (~6 weeks), sparse global representation of MARV.A.1 sequences and low sequence divergence. Strengthening regional sequencing capacity and integrating genomic surveillance within a One Health framework will be essential for timely detection and containment of filovirus and other outbreaks. The Ethiopian event underscores MARV’s ability to emerge in previously unrecognized ecological niches and reinforces the need for sustained preparedness against emerging pathogens. analysis_zh.location_and_population: 暴发 发生在埃塞俄比亚,特别是南埃塞俄比亚地区州阿里地区的金卡。受影响人口包括4,006名调查人员和155名疑似病例,其中确诊病例14例,死亡9例。
analysis_zh.event: 埃塞俄比亚于 2025 年 11 月报告了第一个 暴发 的 马尔堡病毒病,对七个早期病例样本的基因组分析揭示了 暴发 谱系属于 MARV.A.1 分支。暴发 已通过埃塞俄比亚公共卫生研究所 (EPHI) 的逆转录 PCR (RT-PCR) 得到证实。
analysis_zh.scale_impact_and_risk: 暴发导致确诊病例14例,死亡9例,病死率为64%。基因组分析表明 暴发 内的多样性有限,表明单个人畜共患病 跨物种溢出 事件随后是人与人之间的 传播。通过在关键病毒基因中识别出潜在的 突变,强调了进一步传播的风险。
analysis_zh.response_status_and_uncertainty: 埃塞俄比亚政府在确认 MVD 后 48 小时内实施了全面的应急响应,包括接触者追踪、隔离、扩大诊断能力、社区参与以及部署 抗病毒药物 药物和 疫苗。研究结果强调了 基因组监测 对于 暴发 检测和响应的重要性。

news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Monday, November 2, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health No licensed vaccine or drug exists as Marburg virus outbreaks multiply across Africa by October 28, 2026 in Biology, Health Reading Time: 6 mins read 0 No licensed vaccine or drug exists as Marburg virus outbreaks multiply across Africa Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Marburg virus disease has no licensed treatment and no licensed vaccine, yet the virus has triggered a string of outbreaks across Africa in just three years, with Ethiopia confirming its first-ever Marburg outbreak on 14 November 2025. A narrative review published in the journal Discover Viruses on 9 August 2026 synthesises what is currently known about the disease’s epidemiology, virology, pathogenesis, diagnostics and the investigational countermeasures now being evaluated in clinics and laboratories. The review, led by Amit Bansal and colleagues, draws on peer-reviewed literature published up to 13 February 2026, searched in MEDLINE and Embase, and deliberately excludes preprints and unpublished data. Marburg virus disease is a severe and frequently fatal zoonotic haemorrhagic fever caused by two genetically distinct viruses, Marburg virus and Ravn virus, both members of the Filoviridae family and the genus Orthomarburgvirus. Genomic analyses show the two viruses differ by up to 21.3 percent in nucleotide sequence, yet they cause clinically indistinguishable illness. Case fatality rates vary widely, from 24 to 88 percent, reflecting ascertainment bias, outbreak size, access to supportive care and the completeness of surveillance. Globally, more than 600 cases have been recorded since the virus was first identified in August 1967, when laboratory workers in Marburg and Frankfurt in Germany fell ill after handling African green monkeys, with an average case fatality rate of around 50 percent. The review’s authors caution that the case fatality rate is difficult to interpret as a measure of care quality: in a small outbreak where the only detected case is discovered because the patient died, the rate would be 100 percent, a statistical artifact of limited sample size, delayed detection and reporting bias. In larger outbreaks, the rate often falls as a broader spectrum of disease severity is captured. Discover more vaccines Find Vaccines Vaccine Since that first occupational outbreak, subsequent events have occurred predominantly in sub-Saharan Africa, with sporadic imported cases reported in high-income countries. Notable outbreaks include the Democratic Republic of the Congo from 1998 to 2000, Angola in 2005, Equatorial Guinea and Tanzania in 2023, Rwanda in 2024, and Tanzania and Ethiopia in 2025. The 2004–2005 outbreak in Uíge, Angola, disproportionately affected young children, and the intensive care those children required likely catalysed nosocomial and community amplification. Many filovirus outbreaks have been characterised by truncated transmission chains with limited onward propagation, which contrasts sharply with the sustained, widespread community transmission seen during the 2013–2016 West African Ebola epidemic. That difference matters for research: the prolonged Ebola footprint was what made it possible to design and implement robust clinical trials of therapeutics and vaccines, an opportunity Marburg has rarely afforded. Discover more Check Symptoms Study Biology Read Med Journals Track Outbreaks At the molecular level, Marburg virus is a filamentous, enveloped, single-stranded negative-sense RNA virus whose main structural proteins are the glycoprotein, the large polymerase, VP24, VP30, VP35, VP40 and the nucleoprotein. The replication cycle begins when the glycoprotein mediates attachment to host cell receptors, with entry reported to involve macropinocytosis, although clathrin-mediated or alternative pathways may dominate depending on cell type. Once inside endosomes, the GP1 subunit is cleaved by endosomal proteases, an essential step before binding to the Niemann-Pick C1 cholesterol transporter, the principal entry receptor. The GP2 subunit then drives pH-dependent fusion between viral and endosomal membranes, releasing the nucleocapsid into the cytosol, where the genome is transcribed and replicated before new virions bud from the plasma membrane, often at filopodia, in a process driven primarily by VP40. The virus also dismantles the early immune response. VP35 and VP40 likely suppress type I interferon production or signalling, while VP24, unlike its Ebola counterpart, does not block STAT1 nuclear import and is instead associated with modulating Keap1-dependent stress pathways. Infected dendritic cells may fail to mature properly, impairing antigen presentation and cytokine production, and early lymphocyte depletion together with pro-inflammatory cytokine release can potentially contribute to cytokine storm and septic shock. Transmission from animals to humans is suspected to occur through Egyptian fruit bats as the reservoir, with monkeys serving as spillover hosts in laboratory-associated outbreaks, and the virus spreading via the saliva, urine and faeces of infected animals. Once people are infected, they transmit the virus through body fluids including saliva, blood, semen and breast milk, and through contaminated objects such as clothes, bedding and needles. Viremia increases throughout the course of disease, leading to increased shedding, and spread is often associated with caring for the sick and with burial preparations. Discover more vaccine Find Treatments drug Clinically, the incubation period is typically 5 to 12 days, ranging from 2 to 21 days, and begins with fever, myalgia, headache and generalised weakness. By day 3 after symptom onset, patients frequently develop profuse watery diarrhoea, abdominal pain, cramping, nausea and vomiting, and a non-pruritic maculopapular rash, most prominent on the trunk, may appear between days 2 and 7. From around day 5, haemorrhagic manifestations may develop, though not in all patients, including haematemesis, melaena, epistaxis, gingival and vaginal bleeding, and haemorrhage at venepuncture sites. Neurological involvement can include confusion, irritability, aggression, delirium, encephalitis and seizures. Marked biochemical alterations accompany the disease, including elevated liver enzymes, increased creatinine and profound lymphocyte depletion, and later stages may lead to multi-organ failure and death. Viral persistence in immune-privileged sites such as the testes and eyes can lead to orchitis and uveitis during convalescence, sexual transmission is possible months after infection, and recent longitudinal studies have identified persistent cardiometabolic and haematological alterations, such as elevated blood pressure, reticulocytosis and biochemical markers of hepatic and renal stress, even years after recovery. Diagnosis relies on laboratory confirmation because early symptoms are non-specific. RT-PCR is considered the gold standard for detecting Marburg virus RNA, typically targeting conserved genes such as NP, L and GP, with reported analytical sensitivities as low as 5 copies per reaction or 8.6 to 16 RNA copies per assay. ELISA targeting NP, VP40 and GP detects filovirus-specific IgM, visible as early as 2 to 4 days after symptom onset, and IgG, detectable from 8 to 10 days after onset and persisting for up to 2 years. Virus isolation requires a biosafety level 4 laboratory and is not used routinely. The review notes that diagnostic modalities remain limited in accessibility and scalability, particularly in resource-constrained settings, and that no WHO-prequalified and validated Marburg-specific antigen rapid diagnostic test exists for routine clinical deployment. With no approved vaccines or specific antiviral treatments, early intensive supportive care remains the cornerstone of management and was shown to significantly improve patient survival. Intravenous fluid resuscitation, electrolyte correction, analgesia, antipyretics, nutritional support and psychosocial care form the standard package, and follow-up of contacts for early detection, isolation, testing and rapid access to supportive care is key to outbreak management. On the therapeutic front, the monoclonal antibody MBP091, isolated from a Marburg survivor four years after recovery, binds the viral glycoprotein and prevents its interaction with the NPC1 receptor, and a Phase I trial showed it was well tolerated in healthy adult volunteers. Remdesivir, a nucleotide analogue prodrug that inhibits the viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, showed promise in preclinical filovirus models, but human data specific to Marburg are limited, and a randomised controlled trial in the Democratic Republic of the Congo did not demonstrate a survival benefit for remdesivir in Ebola when compared against the monoclonal antibody ZMapp. The WHO-coordinated SOLIDARITY PARTNERS trial is now assessing these therapies for filoviral disease, randomising participants to receive MBP091 or no adjunctive therapy, and a 10-day course of remdesivir or no adjunctive therapy, with a host-directed intervention arm currently inactive. During Rwanda’s 2024 outbreak, frontline healthcare workers were offered both agents under expanded access and clinical trial protocols: remdesivir was administered intravenously to 52 patients, including all who were critically ill, and MBP091 was given to 10 patients, six under expanded access and four enrolled in the WHO-coordinated randomised trial. Early clinical observations indicated that treated patients showed signs of improvement, but the authors stress that because of non-randomisation other factors may have contributed to the differences seen between treated and untreated patients. Rwanda also marked the first time post-exposure prophylaxis was administered to a large number of contacts during a filovirus outbreak, with remdesivir given to 150 contacts; no outcome data have been reported for these individuals, and the lack of randomisation warrants caution in interpreting any effect. In preclinical work, the oral prodrug obeldesivir, given for 10 days starting one day after infection, did not prevent disease from developing but showed 80 percent protection against a lethal Marburg challenge in non-human primates, and its efficacy when given later than one day post-infection still needs study. On the vaccine front, no candidate has yet received regulatory approval, and the WHO Technical Advisory Group has prioritised four viral-vectored candidates encoding the Marburg surface glycoprotein, two based on vesicular stomatitis virus and two on non-replicating chimpanzee adenoviruses. An adenovirus-vectored vaccine developed by the Sabin Vaccine Institute has advanced furthest, demonstrating immunogenicity and safety in human trials, and a Phase I trial in the United States reported binding antibody responses in 95 percent of 40 healthy adult participants at one month, with 70 percent retaining elevated titres at one year. Phase II trials are underway in Uganda, Kenya and the United States, and Oxford University launched a first-in-human trial of its ChAdOx1 Marburg vaccine, which was given to 1,710 frontline workers and high-risk contacts during the 2024 Rwanda outbreak under emergency use authorisation in a phase 2 trial. DNA vaccines required three doses for peak antibody titres, with only 11 percent retaining antibodies at six months, while mRNA vaccines encoding the Marburg glycoprotein have shown promising results in animal models, including complete protection at low doses under specific experimental conditions, though human trials have not yet commenced. The review’s authors conclude that given the sporadic nature of outbreaks, targeted post-exposure measures may be more feasible than widespread pre-exposure immunisation, and that strengthening global preparedness will require integrated surveillance, rapid clinical trial frameworks and equitable access to vaccines and antivirals. On the therapeutic front, the monoclonal antibody MBP091, isolated from a Marburg survivor four years after recovery, binds the viral glycoprotein and prevents its interaction with the NPC1 receptor, and a Phase I trial showed it was well tolerated in healthy adult volunteers. Remdesivir, a nucleotide analogue prodrug that inhibits the viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, showed promise in preclinical filovirus models, but human data specific to Marburg are limited, and a randomised controlled trial in the Democratic Republic of the Congo did not demonstrate a survival benefit for remdesivir in Ebola when compared against the monoclonal antibody ZMapp. The WHO-coordinated SOLIDARITY PARTNERS trial is now assessing these therapies for filoviral disease, randomising participants to receive MBP091 or no adjunctive therapy, and a 10-day course of remdesivir or no adjunctive therapy, with a host-directed intervention arm currently inactive. During Rwanda’s 2024 outbreak, frontline healthcare workers were offered both agents under expanded access and clinical trial protocols: remdesivir was administered intravenously to 52 patients, including all who were critically ill, and MBP091 was given to 10 patients, six under expanded access and four enrolled in the WHO-coordinated randomised trial. Early clinical observations indicated that treated patients showed signs of improvement, but the authors stress that because of non-randomisation other factors may have contributed to the differences seen between treated and untreated patients. Rwanda also marked the first time post-exposure prophylaxis was administered to a large number of contacts during a filovirus outbreak, with remdesivir given to 150 contacts; no outcome data have been reported for these individuals, and the lack of randomisation warrants caution in interpreting any effect. In preclinical work, the oral prodrug obeldesivir, given for 10 days starting one day after infection, did not prevent disease from developing but showed 80 percent protection against a lethal Marburg challenge in non-human primates, and its efficacy when given later than one day post-infection still needs study. On the vaccine front, no candidate has yet received regulatory approval, and the WHO Technical Advisory Group has prioritised four viral-vectored candidates encoding the Marburg surface glycoprotein, two based on vesicular stomatitis virus and two on non-replicating chimpanzee adenoviruses. An adenovirus-vectored vaccine developed by the Sabin Vaccine Institute has advanced furthest, demonstrating immunogenicity and safety in human trials, and a Phase I trial in the United States reported binding antibody responses in 95 percent of 40 healthy adult participants at one month, with 70 percent retaining elevated titres at one year. Phase II trials are underway in Uganda, Kenya and the United States, and Oxford University launched a first-in-human trial of its ChAdOx1 Marburg vaccine, which was given to 1,710 frontline workers and high-risk contacts during the 2024 Rwanda outbreak under emergency use authorisation in a phase 2 trial. DNA vaccines required three doses for peak antibody titres, with only 11 percent retaining antibodies at six months, while mRNA vaccines encoding the Marburg glycoprotein have shown promising results in animal models, including complete protection at low doses under specific experimental conditions, though human trials have not yet commenced. The review’s authors conclude that given the sporadic nature of outbreaks, targeted post-exposure measures may be more feasible than widespread pre-exposure immunisation, and that strengthening global preparedness will require integrated surveillance, rapid clinical trial frameworks and equitable access to vaccines and antivirals. analysis.time: The article was published on 2026-10-28. The event date is 14 November 2025, when Ethiopia confirmed its first-ever Marburg outbreak. The review was published on 9 August 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: The outbreaks have occurred across Africa, including Ethiopia, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Angola, Equatorial Guinea, Tanzania, Rwanda, and others. The affected population includes humans and animals, with transmission occurring through body fluids and contaminated objects.
analysis.event: Marburg virus outbreaks have been reported across Africa, with Ethiopia confirming its first-ever outbreak on 14 November 2025. The article states that no licensed vaccine or drug exists for the disease, and the review highlights the challenges in understanding the disease's epidemiology and treatment options.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Since the virus was first identified in 1967, more than 600 cases have been recorded globally, with an average case fatality rate of around 50 percent. Case fatality rates vary widely, from 24 to 88 percent, depending on factors such as outbreak size, access to supportive care, and surveillance completeness. The disease is a severe and frequently fatal zoonotic haemorrhagic fever.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The review synthesises current knowledge about the disease and its countermeasures, but no licensed vaccine or drug exists. The article notes that the lack of a vaccine or treatment has hindered efforts to control outbreaks. The review excludes preprints and unpublished data, and the case fatality rate is difficult to interpret as a measure of care quality due to reporting bias.

analysis.brief_en: The article published on 2026-10-28 by Bioengineer.org highlights the ongoing Marburg virus outbreaks across Africa, emphasizing the absence of a licensed vaccine or drug. Ethiopia confirmed its first-ever Marburg outbreak on 14 November 2025, and the virus has been responsible for multiple outbreaks in sub-Saharan Africa since its initial identification in 1967. The review published in Discover Viruses on 9 August 2026, led by Amit Bansal and colleagues, synthesizes current knowledge about the disease's epidemiology, virology, and treatment options, drawing on peer-reviewed literature up to 13 February 2026. The review notes that Marburg virus disease is a severe and frequently fatal zoonotic haemorrhagic fever, with case fatality rates ranging from 24 to 88 percent. These rates are influenced by factors such as outbreak size, access to supportive care, and surveillance completeness. The article also mentions that the virus causes clinically indistinguishable illness from Ravn virus, both members of the Filoviridae family. Despite the severity of the disease, no licensed vaccine or drug exists, and the lack of robust clinical trials has limited the development of effective treatments. The review underscores the challenges in interpreting case fatality rates due to reporting bias and limited sample sizes, particularly in small outbreaks where only a few cases are detected. The article further notes that the virus spreads through body fluids and contaminated objects, and outbreaks have been associated with healthcare practices and burial rituals. The absence of a vaccine or treatment remains a critical issue in managing Marburg virus outbreaks.

disease,MVD)暴发,病例致死率为64%。研究人员报告了对来自7例早期病例的7个近完整马尔堡病毒(Marburg virus,MARV)基因组的分析。此次暴发株属于MARV.A.1分支,该分支与历史人类病例及蝙蝠来源的基因组密切相关。这7个基因组之间的高核苷酸同一性表明,在一次人畜共患溢出事件后发生了人与人之间的传播。这些发现凸显了基因组监测在疫情检测、应对和防范中的重要性。 马尔堡病毒病(Marburg virus disease,MVD)是一种由马尔堡病毒(Marburg virus,MARV)引起的高致死性人畜共患感染,病例致死率可达23%至90%。2025年11月,埃塞俄比亚报告了该国首次MVD暴发,病例致死率为64%,亟需通过基因组学手段明确病毒来源、传播动态及进化特征,以支持疫情应对。论文发表于《自然·微生物学》(Nature Microbiology),研究人员对7例早期病例的7个近完整病毒基因组进行了测序和整合分析,为疫情监测和干预策略提供了关键依据。 索取T 细胞活化抗体最新资料 领 取 研究人员在埃塞俄比亚公共卫生研究所(EPHI)对7例经逆转录PCR(RT–PCR)确认的病例样本进行了全基因组测序,并获得覆盖度≥30×、可置信共识序列覆盖>90%的基因组。这些基因组与全球公开的103条正马尔堡病毒(Orthomarburgvirus)全基因组序列整合,构成包含110条序列、跨越13个国家(1967至2025年)的数据集,用以开展系统发育和进化分析。主要技术方法包括:使用Illumina RNA Prep with Enrichment(Viral Surveillance Panel 2)进行文库制备,并在NovaSeq X Plus和MiSeq平台测序;原始读段经fastp质控和修剪、HOSTILE去除人类宿主序列后,以BWA-MEM比对至MARV参考基因组(NC_001608.3),利用iVar完成变异检测和一致性序列组装;随后使用MAFFT进行多序列比对,IQ-TREE构建最大似然系统发育树,TempEst评估时间信号,并采用BEAST进行贝叶斯时间尺度系统发育推断,同时计算谱系定义的单核苷酸多态性(SNP)及dN/dS比值。 研究结果部分归纳如下: - 基因组特征与系统发育:最大似然系统发育分析显示,7条埃塞俄比亚序列构成一个位于MARV.A.1分支内的单系谱系,与历史人类病例和蝙蝠来源序列关系密切。基因组GC含量为40.2%至41.0%,谱系内序列间仅存在0–6个SNP,表明各病毒基因组高度一致。 - 时间尺度进化分析:贝叶斯推断检测到显著的时间信号(R2=0.56,1.75×10?4 替换/位点/年)。埃塞俄比亚谱系与2008年乌干达Python洞感染的人类分离株JN408064(“Leiden”株)最近,两者最近共同祖先(tMRCA)估计为1994年9月(95%最高后验密度区间:1993年1月至1996年4月);与最接近的蝙蝠分离株JX458853和JX458858(2008–2009年采自Python洞)的tMRCA估计为1990年9月(95%最高后验密度区间:1987年4月至1994年2月)。 - 基因组多样性与选择压力:埃塞俄比亚谱系共鉴定出148个谱系定义替换,其中110个位于编码序列(CDS)内,包括28个非同义替换和82个同义替换;38个位于基因间隔区。GP基因是主要分歧热点,包含13个固定非同义替换,如受体结合域的Q205K、粘蛋白样结构域的11个替换(K222N、D250N、A284T、S291P、P295L、N310D、G317D、H336R、T343I、K465E、S485P)以及膜融合区的N501H。VP35含1个非同义替换(S193A);L基因含9个非同义替换(A115V、I359V、I1643T、Q1787R、P1796S、D1806N、R2091K、K2156Q、V2278A),为第二高值;NP和VP基因多样性极低。所有基因的dN/dS<1,提示强烈的纯化选择约束。 - 流行病学与传播推断:流行病学调查支持疫情起源于单次人畜共患溢出事件,最可能的指示病例于2025年10月死亡,在11月12日至24日期间病毒在密切接触者中传播。SNP系统发生树显示T2786C定义了分别源自患者VHF004和VHF060的两个衍生分支,并存在VHF003的T5774C、VHF023的T11337C、VHF045的A2747T等私有突变。由于仅有7个基因组,有限的数据限制了对传播链完整性的确认。 讨论部分指出,埃塞俄比亚谱系的高保守性与近期卢旺达和坦桑尼亚暴发一致,而1998–2000年刚果民主共和国暴发则涉及多次独立溢出。与历史MARV.A.1序列的紧密关系提示该分支在东非和中非长期存在,可能依赖果蝠(Rousettus aegyptiacus)储存并偶发溢出。约30年的分歧时间提示病毒可能最近由邻国引入,也可能已在埃塞俄比亚蝙蝠种群中隐匿传播数十年,需要纵向监测加以区分。此外,病毒进化速率较慢,使这些毒株可能成为治疗药物和疫苗的稳定靶点;相关基因组信息实际指导了瑞德西韦和Sabin cAd3-MARV疫苗在疫情期间的治疗与预防使用。同时,研究存在样本量小、暴发持续时间短(约6周)、全球MARV.A.1序列稀疏以及HPD区间较宽等局限性。 研究结论可翻译为:对埃塞俄比亚MARV的基因组特征分析揭示了一个与东非分支密切相关的谱系,很可能起源于一次人畜共患溢出事件。基因组流行病学为进化稳定性、潜在感染来源和干预策略提供了可操作的信息。然而,这些发现应谨慎解读。加强区域测序能力并将基因组监测纳入“One Health”(同一健康)框架,对于及时发现和遏制丝状病毒及其他病原体暴发至关重要。埃塞俄比亚事件凸显了MARV在先前未被识别的生态位中出现的能力,并强化了对新发病原体持续防范的必要性。 马尔堡病毒病(Marburg virus disease,MVD)是一种由马尔堡病毒(Marburg 讨论部分指出,埃塞俄比亚谱系的高保守性与近期卢旺达和坦桑尼亚暴发一致,而1998–2000年刚果民主共和国暴发则涉及多次独立溢出。与历史MARV.A.1序列的紧密关系提示该分支在东非和中非长期存在,可能依赖果蝠(Rousettus aegyptiacus)储存并偶发溢出。约30年的分歧时间提示病毒可能最近由邻国引入,也可能已在埃塞俄比亚蝙蝠种群中隐匿传播数十年,需要纵向监测加以区分。此外,病毒进化速率较慢,使这些毒株可能成为治疗药物和疫苗的稳定靶点;相关基因组信息实际指导了瑞德西韦和Sabin virus,MARV)引起的高致死性人畜共患感染,病例致死率可达23%至90%。2025年11月,埃塞俄比亚报告了该国首次MVD暴发,病例致死率为64%,亟需通过基因组学手段明确病毒来源、传播动态及进化特征,以支持疫情应对。论文发表于《自然·微生物学》(Nature Microbiology),研究人员对7例早期病例的7个近完整病毒基因组进行了测序和整合分析,为疫情监测和干预策略提供了关键依据。研究人员在埃塞俄比亚公共卫生研究所(EPHI)对7例经逆转录PCR(RT–PCR)确认的病例样本进行了全基因组测序,并获得覆盖度≥30×、可置信共识序列覆盖>90%的基因组。这些基因组与全球公开的103条正马尔堡病毒(Orthomarburgvirus)全基因组序列整合,构成包含110条序列、跨越13个国家(1967至2025年)的数据集,用以开展系统发育和进化分析。主要技术方法包括:使用Illumina A new genomic analysis, published in Nature Microbiology, reports seven near-complete Marburg virus genomes recovered from seven early cases in that outbreak. The sequences show that the outbreak lineage belonged to the MARV.A.1 clade, a group closely related to genomes from historical human cases and from bats. High nucleotide identity across the seven genomes points to human-to-human transmission following a zoonotic spillover event, in which the virus jumped from an animal reservoir into people and then spread between them. The authors argue that the findings underline the value of genomic surveillance for outbreak detection, response and preparedness. The work was carried out by researchers from the Ethiopian Public Health Institute (EPHI) and the Federal Ministry of Health, together with long-standing collaborators at the Amsterdam Institute for Global Health and Development, Amsterdam University and McMaster University, through the EpiGen-Ethiopia project, which is building scalable capacity for pathogen genomic surveillance in Ethiopia for emerging and re-emerging infectious diseases. The study was approved by the EPHI Institutional Review Board (EPHI-IRB-633-2025). Given the emergency situation, verbal consent was received from all patients included in the report, and all collected samples were anonymized to prevent the identification of any individual. The researchers were involved in all stages of the work, including study design, epidemiological investigation, community engagement, data collection, analysis and manuscript preparation. Discover more genomic Genomic genomes The samples at the heart of the study were blood specimens collected from patients suspected of having viral haemorrhagic fever, presenting with symptoms such as high fever, severe headache, muscle pain, fatigue, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea and bleeding. The samples were transported under standard operating procedures for infectious material to the EPHI in Addis Ababa. There, at the Integrated Pathogen Genomics and Bioinformatics Facility for Surveillance and Research, they were inactivated inside a fixed-film isolator using 100% ethanol at five times the sample volume. RNA was then extracted with a Qiagen kit inside a class III biosafety cabinet, following the manufacturer’s instructions, with lysing and purification buffers and a final elution step. The extracted RNA was screened by multiplex RT–PCR for dengue, Zika, Chikungunya, Yellow Fever, Ebola and Marburg viruses. Discover more Check Symptoms Read Med Journals Track Outbreaks genome Of the specimens screened, 14 were RT–PCR-positive for Marburg virus. Not all of these yielded usable sequence data: two genomes had less than 52% breadth of coverage and five samples were unavailable for processing, leaving seven samples that underwent whole-genome sequencing. Library preparation used the Illumina RNA Prep with Enrichment workflow with the Viral Surveillance Panel 2. In this workflow, RNA was reverse transcribed to cDNA, enzymatically fragmented and amplified to add indexes and adaptor sequences. Library concentrations were measured with a Qubit 1× dsDNA High Sensitivity assay before enrichment, and target enrichment was performed by hybridization with capture probes from the Viral Surveillance Panel 2, followed by capture with Streptavidin Magnetic Beads 3, elution, amplification and purification with Illumina purification beads. The enriched libraries were normalized, pooled in equimolar concentrations and diluted to the appropriate loading concentration for sequencing. Two libraries were diluted with NovaSeq X series Pre-Load Buffer to a final concentration of 150 pM and sequenced on an Illumina NovaSeq X Plus platform using 2 × 150-bp paired-end reads. The remaining libraries were normalized to 10 pM and sequenced on an Illumina MiSeq platform using 2 × 300-bp paired-end reads. All pooled libraries were denatured with freshly prepared 0.2 N sodium hydroxide before sequencing. These details matter because they document how a national public health laboratory, sequencing in-country, produced near-complete viral genomes during an active outbreak. The bioinformatic pipeline began with quality control and trimming of raw paired-end reads using fastp v0.23.4, removing low-quality bases (Phred below 20), adaptor sequences, poly-G/poly-X tails, low-complexity regions and reads shorter than 50 base pairs. Host-derived reads were removed using HOSTILE v2.0.2, which aligns reads against the human reference genome GRCh38.p13; only read pairs that did not align to the human genome were retained. Non-host reads were then mapped to the Marburg virus reference genome (accession NC_001608.3) using BWA-MEM v0.7.18 in short-read mode with default Illumina-optimized parameters. The reference is the complete genome of the Musoke strain, derived from the 1980 outbreak in Kenya, a 19,112-base-pair sequence first sequenced in 1992. BAM files were sorted and indexed with SAMtools v1.17, and coverage, alignment quality and duplication rates were assessed with Qualimap v2.2.2. Variants were called with iVar v1.3.1 combined with SAMtools mpileup, applying a minimum base quality of 20 and a variant frequency threshold of 0.03, generating per-sample consensus genomes with ambiguous positions coded as N. Consensus sequences were aligned with MAFFT v7.520 (L-INS-i). The final comparative dataset included 110 Marburg virus whole-genome sequences sampled between 1967 and 2025, spanning 13 countries: the DRC (n = 30), Rwanda (n = 18), Uganda (n = 17), Angola (n = 16), Ethiopia (n = 7), Sierra Leone (n = 6), Tanzania (n = 5), Kenya (n = 3), South Africa (n = 2), Ghana (n = 2), Guinea (n = 2), Germany (n = 1) and the Netherlands (n = 1). Clade assignments and quality control were performed with Nextclade v2.15.2, and phylogenies were reconstructed with IQ-TREE v2.2.5 under the best-fit substitution model identified by ModelFinder, with ultrafast bootstrap approximation for branch support. To assess whether the data carried a usable temporal signal, the team performed root-to-tip regression analysis with TempEst v1.5.3 on the maximum-likelihood phylogeny, optimizing the tree root to maximize the correlation between root-to-tip genetic distance and sampling date, using RAVV as a true outgroup that was pruned before the regression and restricting the analysis to global Marburg virus genomes, following a previously validated approach. Time-scaled phylogenies were inferred with BEAST v10.5.0 under the HKY nucleotide substitution model with empirical base frequencies, selected by Bayesian information criterion comparison in ModelFinder. A fixed local clock model was used: a fixed substitution rate of 1 × 10−3 substitutions per site per year was assumed for the defined outbreak clade, representing a plausible evolutionary rate for an RNA virus during the early stage of an outbreak, while the deeper evolutionary history was allowed to evolve under a lognormal relaxed clock prior centred on 5 × 10−4 substitutions per site per year, reflecting the lower rate expected outside the rapid outbreak phase. The demographic model was similarly two-phased. A coalescent Bayesian SkyGrid tree prior allowed effective population size to vary flexibly through time; the subtree from the Ethiopian lineage tMRCA to the present was modelled with an exponential growth coalescent prior, reflecting the rapid expansion expected during an outbreak, while the earlier, deeper history was modelled with a constant-population-size coalescent prior, assuming stable viral population dynamics before the emergence of the outbreak lineage. Two independent MCMC chains were run for 100 million states each, sampling every 10,000 steps, with the initial 10% discarded as burn-in. Convergence was evaluated visually in Tracer v1.7.2 and quantitatively through effective sample size calculations, with ESS values above 200 considered indicative of adequate mixing; all estimated parameters achieved ESS values above the recommended threshold. The remaining posterior samples, 45,001 per chain, were combined with LogCombiner v10.5.0, and tMRCAs were calculated as posterior mean node heights with TreeAnnotator v10.5.0, converted to calendar years using the decimal year of the most recent tip in the dataset. Beyond the phylogeny, the researchers identified specific lineage-defining SNPs in the Ethiopian samples from multiple sequence alignments, mapped them to genes using reference GenBank annotations, translated them into amino acid changes and classified them as synonymous or non-synonymous. They also calculated nucleotide diversity, Watterson’s theta and segregating sites for the Ethiopian sequences, and estimated gene-level dN/dS ratios. The genome sequences generated in the study are publicly available on Pathoplexus under the accession numbers PP_00731R3.4, PP_00730R4.4, PP_00731Q5.4, PP_00731P7.4, PP_00730Q6.4, PP_0072YT4.4 and PP_0072ZR7.4, and all analysis code and data are available via GitHub. Taken together, the seven near-complete genomes, their placement in the MARV.A.1 clade and their high mutual nucleotide identity provide a genomic picture of the earliest phase of Ethiopia’s first recorded Marburg virus disease outbreak: a zoonotic spillover followed by human-to-human transmission, documented by genomic surveillance conducted within the affected country. news.source_body_en: In November 2025, Ethiopia experienced its first outbreak of Marburg virus disease, with a reported case fatality rate of 64%. A genomic analysis, published on October 29, 2026, revealed that the outbreak lineage belonged to the MARV.A.1 clade, indicating post-spillover human-to-human transmission. The study, conducted by researchers from the Ethiopian Public Health Institute (EPHI), the Federal Ministry of Health, and international collaborators, involved sequencing seven near-complete Marburg virus genomes from early cases. These genomes were obtained from patients suspected of having viral haemorrhagic fever, presenting with symptoms like high fever and muscle pain. The analysis was part of the EpiGen-Ethiopia project, which focuses on building genomic surveillance capacity for emerging infectious diseases. The findings emphasize the value of genomic surveillance in outbreak detection and response, as well as the importance of biosafety protocols and ethical practices in handling infectious samples.

news.content: Affordable, accessible vaccines & antibodies We are a global nonprofit biomedical research organization that develops vaccines and antibodies for HIV, tuberculosis, and emerging infectious diseases. About us Our approach We take a full-circle approach to product development, from the grassroots level to the lab to legislative bodies. Mission To translate scientific discoveries into affordable, globally accessible public health solutions. Vision A world where all people have equitable access to innovative vaccines and therapeutics. Our health areas - HIV - Tuberculosis - Lassa virus - Marburg virus - Sudan virus - Bundibugyo virus HIV The challenge HIV/AIDS remains one of the deadliest infectious diseases, with 1.4 million people acquiring HIV in 2024. Given the complexities of HIV, traditional approaches to vaccine development have so far failed to result in a preventive vaccine. However, a vaccine is still needed to bring a true end to the HIV pandemic. Source: UNAIDS Our solution IAVI scientists and our collaborators are developing next-generation HIV vaccines to address the challenges of HIV vaccine design. Together, we have pioneered promising new vaccination strategies and the discovery of broadly neutralizing antibodies (bnAbs) against HIV. IAVI and our partners are developing HIV bnAbs to prevent HIV acquisition in infants. Tuberculosis The challenge Tuberculosis (TB) is the world’s leading infectious disease killer. In 2024, 10.7 million people fell ill with TB and 1.23 million people died of TB disease. The only available TB vaccine is the century-old Bacille Calmette-Guérin, or BCG. While this vaccine has efficacy in protecting against severe TB disease in infants and young children, it is largely ineffective in adolescents and adults, among whom most transmission and disease occurs. Source: WHO Our solution IAVI works across our global hubs with a diverse network of partners to advance promising TB vaccine candidates from discovery through clinical trials, and eventually, to post-licensure access. Our work extends to policy and advocacy initiatives that support TB vaccine development and access in regions where new vaccines are needed most. Lassa virus The challenge Lassa virus is an arenavirus that causes Lassa fever, an acute viral hemorrhagic illness endemic to West Africa that causes significant annual outbreaks of disease. Lassa fever is difficult to diagnose, and surveillance data is limited. Current estimates range from 300,000 to 500,000 cases and 5,000 related deaths each year. No licensed vaccines for Lassa fever exist. Source: WHO Our solution IAVI is developing a single-dose vaccine candidate for Lassa that is based on a recombinant vesicular stomatitis virus (rVSV) vector. This technology is similar to that underlying an approved Ebola Zaire virus vaccine. In 2024, IAVI’s Lassa vaccine candidate became the first Lassa vaccine to enter Phase 2 clinical trials, launched in three West African countries. This trial builds on a Phase 1 clinical trial that showed the candidate vaccine was well tolerated and immunogenic over a wide dose range. IAVI also conducts Lassa epidemiological studies, modeling, and community engagement to support future vaccine access. Marburg virus The challenge Marburg virus is a filovirus and the causative agent of Marburg virus disease (MVD), which has a case fatality rate of up to 88%. Marburg virus has the capacity to cause deadly outbreaks and is a potential bioterror threat. No vaccines or antiviral treatments are approved for MVD. A Marburg vaccine is urgently needed to respond to future outbreaks. Source: WHO Our solution IAVI is developing a vaccine candidate for Marburg that is based on a recombinant vesicular stomatitis virus (rVSV) vector. This technology is similar to that underlying an approved Ebola Zaire virus vaccine. Preclinical data demonstrates that IAVI’s Marburg vaccine candidate is highly protective in an animal model with one dose. Sudan virus The challenge Sudan virus (SUDV) is a filovirus and causes outbreaks of Ebola disease, most recently in 2025 in Uganda. Case fatality rates of Ebola disease caused by SUDV have varied from 41% to 100% in past outbreaks. The licensed vaccine for Ebola Zaire virus does not provide cross protection against the Sudan strain. A SUDV vaccine is urgently needed to prevent and respond to future outbreaks. Source: WHO Our solution IAVI is developing a vaccine candidate for SUDV that is based on a recombinant vesicular stomatitis virus (rVSV) vector similar to the technology underlying an approved Ebola Zaire virus vaccine. During an Ebola outbreak starting in January 2025 in Uganda, the WHO prioritized IAVI’s SUDV vaccine candidate for a ring vaccination trial and delivered the first vaccinations just four days after the outbreak was declared as part of a comprehensive public health response. Bundibugyo virus The challenge Bundibugyo virus (BDBV) is a filovirus that has caused only three known outbreaks to date. The outbreak that began in Democratic Republic of Congo in May 2026 quickly turned into an epidemic and was determined by the WHO to be a Public Health Emergency of International Concern. There are no licensed vaccines or specific treatments for BDBV. The case fatality rate of BDBV disease ranges between 30-50%. Our solution At the outset of the outbreak in May 2026, IAVI quickly brought a BDBV vaccine candidate in house. It is based on the same recombinant vesicular stomatitis virus (rVSV) vector as our other emerging infectious diseases vaccine candidates as well as the approved Ebola Zaire virus vaccine. The WHO has prioritized development of this vaccine during the epidemic as the most promising candidate in the pipeline. Our locations IAVI Africa - Cape Town Office, South Africa - Nairobi Office, Kenya IAVI Europe - Amsterdam Office, The Netherlands - Human Immunology Lab, London, U.K. IAVI India - Gurugram, Haryana Office - Antibody Translational Research Program, IAVI-THSTI, Faridabad IAVI U.S. - New York Office - Vaccine Design & Development Lab, New York - Neutralizing Antibody Center, California

supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Monday, November 2, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health No licensed vaccine or drug exists as Marburg virus outbreaks multiply across Africa by October 28, 2026 in Biology, Health Reading Time: 6 mins read 0 No licensed vaccine or drug exists as Marburg virus outbreaks multiply across Africa Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Marburg virus disease has no licensed treatment and no licensed vaccine, yet the virus has triggered a string of outbreaks across Africa in just three years, with Ethiopia confirming its first-ever Marburg outbreak on 14 November 2025. A narrative review published in the journal Discover Viruses on 9 August 2026 synthesises what is currently known about the disease’s epidemiology, virology, pathogenesis, diagnostics and the investigational countermeasures now being evaluated in clinics and laboratories. The review, led by Amit Bansal and colleagues, draws on peer-reviewed literature published up to 13 February 2026, searched in MEDLINE and Embase, and deliberately excludes preprints and unpublished data. Marburg virus disease is a severe and frequently fatal zoonotic haemorrhagic fever caused by two genetically distinct viruses, Marburg virus and Ravn virus, both members of the Filoviridae family and the genus Orthomarburgvirus. Genomic analyses show the two viruses differ by up to 21.3 percent in nucleotide sequence, yet they cause clinically indistinguishable illness. Case fatality rates vary widely, from 24 to 88 percent, reflecting ascertainment bias, outbreak size, access to supportive care and the completeness of surveillance. Globally, more than 600 cases have been recorded since the virus was first identified in August 1967, when laboratory workers in Marburg and Frankfurt in Germany fell ill after handling African green monkeys, with an average case fatality rate of around 50 percent. The review’s authors caution that the case fatality rate is difficult to interpret as a measure of care quality: in a small outbreak where the only detected case is discovered because the patient died, the rate would be 100 percent, a statistical artifact of limited sample size, delayed detection and reporting bias. In larger outbreaks, the rate often falls as a broader spectrum of disease severity is captured. Since that first occupational outbreak, subsequent events have occurred predominantly in sub-Saharan Africa, with sporadic imported cases reported in high-income countries. Notable outbreaks include the Democratic Republic of the Congo from 1998 to 2000, Angola in 2005, Equatorial Guinea and Tanzania in 2023, Rwanda in 2024, and Tanzania and Ethiopia in 2025. The 2004–2005 outbreak in Uíge, Angola, disproportionately affected young children, and the intensive care those children required likely catalysed nosocomial and community amplification. Many filovirus outbreaks have been characterised by truncated transmission chains with limited onward propagation, which contrasts sharply with the sustained, widespread community transmission seen during the 2013–2016 West African Ebola epidemic. That difference matters for research: the prolonged Ebola footprint was what made it possible to design and implement robust clinical trials of therapeutics and vaccines, an opportunity Marburg has rarely afforded. At the molecular level, Marburg virus is a filamentous, enveloped, single-stranded negative-sense RNA virus whose main structural proteins are the glycoprotein, the large polymerase, VP24, VP30, VP35, VP40 and the nucleoprotein. The replication cycle begins when the glycoprotein mediates attachment to host cell receptors, with entry reported to involve macropinocytosis, although clathrin-mediated or alternative pathways may dominate depending on cell type. Once inside endosomes, the GP1 subunit is cleaved by endosomal proteases, an essential step before binding to the Niemann-Pick C1 cholesterol transporter, the principal entry receptor. The GP2 subunit then drives pH-dependent fusion between viral and endosomal membranes, releasing the nucleocapsid into the cytosol, where the genome is transcribed and replicated before new virions bud from the plasma membrane, often at filopodia, in a process driven primarily by VP40. The virus also dismantles the early immune response. VP35 and VP40 likely suppress type I interferon production or signalling, while VP24, unlike its Ebola counterpart, does not block STAT1 nuclear import and is instead associated with modulating Keap1-dependent stress pathways. Infected dendritic cells may fail to mature properly, impairing antigen presentation and cytokine production, and early lymphocyte depletion together with pro-inflammatory cytokine release can potentially contribute to cytokine storm and septic shock. Transmission from animals to humans is suspected to occur through Egyptian fruit bats as the reservoir, with monkeys serving as spillover hosts in laboratory-associated outbreaks, and the virus spreading via the saliva, urine and faeces of infected animals. Once people are infected, they transmit the virus through body fluids including saliva, blood, semen and breast milk, and through contaminated objects such as clothes, bedding and needles. Viremia increases throughout the course of disease, leading to increased shedding, and spread is often associated with caring for the sick and with burial preparations. Clinically, the incubation period is typically 5 to 12 days, ranging from 2 to 21 days, and begins with fever, myalgia, headache and generalised weakness. By day 3 after symptom onset, patients frequently develop profuse watery diarrhoea, abdominal pain, cramping, nausea and vomiting, and a non-pruritic maculopapular rash, most prominent on the trunk, may appear between days 2 and 7. From around day 5, haemorrhagic manifestations may develop, though not in all patients, including haematemesis, melaena, epistaxis, gingival and vaginal bleeding, and haemorrhage at venepuncture sites. Neurological involvement can include confusion, irritability, aggression, delirium, encephalitis and seizures. Marked biochemical alterations accompany the disease, including elevated liver enzymes, increased creatinine and profound lymphocyte depletion, and later stages may lead to multi-organ failure and death. Viral persistence in immune-privileged sites such as the testes and eyes can lead to orchitis and uveitis during convalescence, sexual transmission is possible months after infection, and recent longitudinal studies have identified persistent cardiometabolic and haematological alterations, such as elevated blood pressure, reticulocytosis and biochemical markers of hepatic and renal stress, even years after recovery. Diagnosis relies on laboratory confirmation because early symptoms are non-specific. RT-PCR is considered the gold standard for detecting Marburg virus RNA, typically targeting conserved genes such as NP, L and GP, with reported analytical sensitivities as low as 5 copies per reaction or 8.6 to 16 RNA copies per assay. ELISA targeting NP, VP40 and GP detects filovirus-specific IgM, visible as early as 2 to 4 days after symptom onset, and IgG, detectable from 8 to 10 days after onset and persisting for up to 2 years. Virus isolation requires a biosafety level 4 laboratory and is not used routinely. The review notes that diagnostic modalities remain limited in accessibility and scalability, particularly in resource-constrained settings, and that no WHO-prequalified and validated Marburg-specific antigen rapid diagnostic test exists for routine clinical deployment. With no approved vaccines or specific antiviral treatments, early intensive supportive care remains the cornerstone of management and was shown to significantly improve patient survival. Intravenous fluid resuscitation, electrolyte correction, analgesia, antipyretics, nutritional support and psychosocial care form the standard package, and follow-up of contacts for early detection, isolation, testing and rapid access to supportive care is key to outbreak management. On the therapeutic front, the monoclonal antibody MBP091, isolated from a Marburg survivor four years after recovery, binds the viral glycoprotein and prevents its interaction with the NPC1 receptor, and a Phase I trial showed it was well tolerated in healthy adult volunteers. Remdesivir, a nucleotide analogue prodrug that inhibits the viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, showed promise in preclinical filovirus models, but human data specific to Marburg are limited, and a randomised controlled trial in the Democratic Republic of the Congo did not demonstrate a survival benefit for remdesivir in Ebola when compared against the monoclonal antibody ZMapp. The WHO-coordinated SOLIDARITY PARTNERS trial is now assessing these therapies for filoviral disease, randomising participants to receive MBP091 or no adjunctive therapy, and a 10-day course of remdesivir or no adjunctive therapy, with a host-directed intervention arm currently inactive. During Rwanda’s 2024 outbreak, frontline healthcare workers were offered both agents under expanded access and clinical trial protocols: remdesivir was administered intravenously to 52 patients, including all who were critically ill, and MBP091 was given to 10 patients, six under expanded access and four enrolled in the WHO-coordinated randomised trial. Early clinical observations indicated that treated patients showed signs of improvement, but the authors stress that because of non-randomisation other factors may have contributed to the differences seen between treated and untreated patients. Rwanda also marked the first time post-exposure prophylaxis was administered to a large number of contacts during a filovirus outbreak, with remdesivir given to 150 contacts; no outcome data have been reported for these individuals, and the lack of randomisation warrants caution in interpreting any effect. In preclinical work, the oral prodrug obeldesivir, given for 10 days starting one day after infection, did not prevent disease from developing but showed 80 percent protection against a lethal Marburg challenge in non-human primates, and its efficacy when given later than one day post-infection still needs study. On the vaccine front, no candidate has yet received regulatory approval, and the WHO Technical Advisory Group has prioritised four viral-vectored candidates encoding the Marburg surface glycoprotein, two based on vesicular stomatitis virus and two on non-replicating chimpanzee adenoviruses. An adenovirus-vectored vaccine developed by the Sabin Vaccine Institute has advanced furthest, demonstrating immunogenicity and safety in human trials, and a Phase I trial in the United States reported binding antibody responses in 95 percent of 40 healthy adult participants at one month, with 70 percent retaining elevated titres at one year. Phase II trials are underway in Uganda, Kenya and the United States, and Oxford University launched a first-in-human trial of its ChAdOx1 Marburg vaccine, which was given to 1,710 frontline workers and high-risk contacts during the 2024 Rwanda outbreak under emergency use authorisation in a phase 2 trial. DNA vaccines required three doses for peak antibody titres, with only 11 percent retaining antibodies at six months, while mRNA vaccines encoding the Marburg glycoprotein have shown promising results in animal models, including complete protection at low doses under specific experimental conditions, though human trials have not yet commenced. The review’s authors conclude that given the sporadic nature of outbreaks, targeted post-exposure measures may be more feasible than widespread pre-exposure immunisation, and that strengthening global preparedness will require integrated surveillance, rapid clinical trial frameworks and equitable access to vaccines and antivirals. supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Monday, November 2, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Biology Genomes from Ethiopia’s first Marburg outbreak reveal post-spillover human transmission by October 29, 2026 in Biology Reading Time: 6 mins read 0 Genomes from Ethiopia's first Marburg outbreak reveal post-spillover human transmission Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram In November 2025, Ethiopia reported its first outbreak of Marburg virus disease, with a case fatality rate of 64%. A new genomic analysis, published in Nature Microbiology, reports seven near-complete Marburg virus genomes recovered from seven early cases in that outbreak. The sequences show that the outbreak lineage belonged to the MARV.A.1 clade, a group closely related to genomes from historical human cases and from bats. High nucleotide identity across the seven genomes points to human-to-human transmission following a zoonotic spillover event, in which the virus jumped from an animal reservoir into people and then spread between them. The authors argue that the findings underline the value of genomic surveillance for outbreak detection, response and preparedness. The work was carried out by researchers from the Ethiopian Public Health Institute (EPHI) and the Federal Ministry of Health, together with long-standing collaborators at the Amsterdam Institute for Global Health and Development, Amsterdam University and McMaster University, through the EpiGen-Ethiopia project, which is building scalable capacity for pathogen genomic surveillance in Ethiopia for emerging and re-emerging infectious diseases. The study was approved by the EPHI Institutional Review Board (EPHI-IRB-633-2025). Given the emergency situation, verbal consent was received from all patients included in the report, and all collected samples were anonymized to prevent the identification of any individual. The researchers were involved in all stages of the work, including study design, epidemiological investigation, community engagement, data collection, analysis and manuscript preparation. The samples at the heart of the study were blood specimens collected from patients suspected of having viral haemorrhagic fever, presenting with symptoms such as high fever, severe headache, muscle pain, fatigue, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea and bleeding. The samples were transported under standard operating procedures for infectious material to the EPHI in Addis Ababa. There, at the Integrated Pathogen Genomics and Bioinformatics Facility for Surveillance and Research, they were inactivated inside a fixed-film isolator using 100% ethanol at five times the sample volume. RNA was then extracted with a Qiagen kit inside a class III biosafety cabinet, following the manufacturer’s instructions, with lysing and purification buffers and a final elution step. The extracted RNA was screened by multiplex RT–PCR for dengue, Zika, Chikungunya, Yellow Fever, Ebola and Marburg viruses. Of the specimens screened, 14 were RT–PCR-positive for Marburg virus. Not all of these yielded usable sequence data: two genomes had less than 52% breadth of coverage and five samples were unavailable for processing, leaving seven samples that underwent whole-genome sequencing. Library preparation used the Illumina RNA Prep with Enrichment workflow with the Viral Surveillance Panel 2. In this workflow, RNA was reverse transcribed to cDNA, enzymatically fragmented and amplified to add indexes and adaptor sequences. Library concentrations were measured with a Qubit 1× dsDNA High Sensitivity assay before enrichment, and target enrichment was performed by hybridization with capture probes from the Viral Surveillance Panel 2, followed by capture with Streptavidin Magnetic Beads 3, elution, amplification and purification with Illumina purification beads. The enriched libraries were normalized, pooled in equimolar concentrations and diluted to the appropriate loading concentration for sequencing. Two libraries were diluted with NovaSeq X series Pre-Load Buffer to a final concentration of 150 pM and sequenced on an Illumina NovaSeq X Plus platform using 2 × 150-bp paired-end reads. The remaining libraries were normalized to 10 pM and sequenced on an Illumina MiSeq platform using 2 × 300-bp paired-end reads. All pooled libraries were denatured with freshly prepared 0.2 N sodium hydroxide before sequencing. These details matter because they document how a national public health laboratory, sequencing in-country, produced near-complete viral genomes during an active outbreak. The bioinformatic pipeline began with quality control and trimming of raw paired-end reads using fastp v0.23.4, removing low-quality bases (Phred below 20), adaptor sequences, poly-G/poly-X tails, low-complexity regions and reads shorter than 50 base pairs. Host-derived reads were removed using HOSTILE v2.0.2, which aligns reads against the human reference genome GRCh38.p13; only read pairs that did not align to the human genome were retained. Non-host reads were then mapped to the Marburg virus reference genome (accession NC_001608.3) using BWA-MEM v0.7.18 in short-read mode with default Illumina-optimized parameters. The reference is the complete genome of the Musoke strain, derived from the 1980 outbreak in Kenya, a 19,112-base-pair sequence first sequenced in 1992. BAM files were sorted and indexed with SAMtools v1.17, and coverage, alignment quality and duplication rates were assessed with Qualimap v2.2.2. Variants were called with iVar v1.3.1 combined with SAMtools mpileup, applying a minimum base quality of 20 and a variant frequency threshold of 0.03, generating per-sample consensus genomes with ambiguous positions coded as N. Consensus sequences were aligned with MAFFT v7.520 (L-INS-i). The final comparative dataset included 110 Marburg virus whole-genome sequences sampled between 1967 and 2025, spanning 13 countries: the DRC (n = 30), Rwanda (n = 18), Uganda (n = 17), Angola (n = 16), Ethiopia (n = 7), Sierra Leone (n = 6), Tanzania (n = 5), Kenya (n = 3), South Africa (n = 2), Ghana (n = 2), Guinea (n = 2), Germany (n = 1) and the Netherlands (n = 1). Clade assignments and quality control were performed with Nextclade v2.15.2, and phylogenies were reconstructed with IQ-TREE v2.2.5 under the best-fit substitution model identified by ModelFinder, with ultrafast bootstrap approximation for branch support. To assess whether the data carried a usable temporal signal, the team performed root-to-tip regression analysis with TempEst v1.5.3 on the maximum-likelihood phylogeny, optimizing the tree root to maximize the correlation between root-to-tip genetic distance and sampling date, using RAVV as a true outgroup that was pruned before the regression and restricting the analysis to global Marburg virus genomes, following a previously validated approach. Time-scaled phylogenies were inferred with BEAST v10.5.0 under the HKY nucleotide substitution model with empirical base frequencies, selected by Bayesian information criterion comparison in ModelFinder. A fixed local clock model was used: a fixed substitution rate of 1 × 10−3 substitutions per site per year was assumed for the defined outbreak clade, representing a plausible evolutionary rate for an RNA virus during the early stage of an outbreak, while the deeper evolutionary history was allowed to evolve under a lognormal relaxed clock prior centred on 5 × 10−4 substitutions per site per year, reflecting the lower rate expected outside the rapid outbreak phase. The demographic model was similarly two-phased. A coalescent Bayesian SkyGrid tree prior allowed effective population size to vary flexibly through time; the subtree from the Ethiopian lineage tMRCA to the present was modelled with an exponential growth coalescent prior, reflecting the rapid expansion expected during an outbreak, while the earlier, deeper history was modelled with a constant-population-size coalescent prior, assuming stable viral population dynamics before the emergence of the outbreak lineage. Two independent MCMC chains were run for 100 million states each, sampling every 10,000 steps, with the initial 10% discarded as burn-in. Convergence was evaluated visually in Tracer v1.7.2 and quantitatively through effective sample size calculations, with ESS values above 200 considered indicative of adequate mixing; all estimated parameters achieved ESS values above the recommended threshold. The remaining posterior samples, 45,001 per chain, were combined with LogCombiner v10.5.0, and tMRCAs were calculated as posterior mean node heights with TreeAnnotator v10.5.0, converted to calendar years using the decimal year of the most recent tip in the dataset. Beyond the phylogeny, the researchers identified specific lineage-defining SNPs in the Ethiopian samples from multiple sequence alignments, mapped them to genes using reference GenBank annotations, translated them into amino acid changes and classified them as synonymous or non-synonymous. They also calculated nucleotide diversity, Watterson’s theta and segregating sites for the Ethiopian sequences, and estimated gene-level dN/dS ratios. The genome sequences generated in the study are publicly available on Pathoplexus under the accession numbers PP_00731R3.4, PP_00730R4.4, PP_00731Q5.4, PP_00731P7.4, PP_00730Q6.4, PP_0072YT4.4 and PP_0072ZR7.4, and all analysis code and data are available via GitHub. Taken together, the seven near-complete genomes, their placement in the MARV.A.1 clade and their high mutual nucleotide identity provide a genomic picture of the earliest phase of Ethiopia’s first recorded Marburg virus disease outbreak: a zoonotic spillover followed by human-to-human transmission, documented by genomic surveillance conducted within the affected country.
